suggestions.title: Witness for the Prosecution
suggestions.description: Your trial shelf so far is 12 Angry Men (a jury locked in one room) and Knives Out (a comedy whodunit); this is the actual courtroom film, and it is the one Agatha Christie wrote. Billy Wilder directed from Christie's own 1953 stage play, which she adapted from her 1925 short story "Traitor's Hands", with the screenplay credited to Wilder and Harry Kurnitz and adapted by Larry Marcus. It was released in 1957, shot in black and white, and staged almost entirely inside the Old Bailey. Charles Laughton is Sir Wilfrid Robarts, a celebrated barrister just out of a heart attack and under doctors' orders not to take a criminal brief, who agrees to defend Leonard Vole (Tyrone Power), a charming man accused of murdering Emily French, a wealthy childless widow who had fallen for him and left him the bulk of her estate. Marlene Dietrich is Christine, Leonard's German wife, who first supplies his alibi and then appears for the prosecution - and Elsa Lanchester, Laughton's real-life wife of more than thirty years, plays his nurse Miss Plimsoll, a running gag built on a thermos she keeps hidden and a brandy she keeps from him. It took six Academy Award nominations - Best Picture, Best Director for Wilder, Best Actor for Laughton, Best Supporting Actress for Lanchester, plus Film Editing and Sound - and won none of them; Lanchester did win the Golden Globe for Best Supporting Actress. The American Film Institute placed it sixth among the ten greatest courtroom dramas. Wilder ends the picture with a card asking the audience not to reveal what happens, and the film earns it: it is built so that you trust exactly the wrong person, twice. It was Tyrone Power's last completed film; he died the following year during the making of Solomon and Sheba. IMDb 8.4.

suggestions.title: Blade Runner
suggestions.description: Blade Runner 2049 has been on this shelf since the start; this is the film it is answering, and the hole it leaves. Ridley Scott directed from a screenplay by Hampton Fancher and David Peoples, adapting Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, and it was released in the United States on 25 June 1982 - two weeks after E.T., into an audience that had just been handed a loveable alien and was not in the mood for this one. Harrison Ford is Rick Deckard, the blade runner pulled out of retirement to "retire" four escaped replicants in a rain-soaked Los Angeles of 2019; Rutger Hauer is Roy Batty, the leader of them, Daryl Hannah is Pris, Joanna Cassidy is Zhora, Brion James is Leon, Sean Young is Rachael, M. Emmet Walsh is Bryant, William Sanderson is J.F. Sebastian and Edward James Olmos is Gaff, who leaves little origami figures behind him. Behind the camera: production design by Lawrence G. Paull with David Snyder, effects supervised by Douglas Trumbull and Richard Yuricich, concept art by Syd Mead, and a score by Vangelis that is half of the film's identity. It was nominated for two Academy Awards, Best Production Design and Best Visual Effects, and lost both. The production was famously hostile - the studio forced in a voice-over and a happy ending after test screenings, Harrison Ford recorded the narration under protest and has never hidden his dislike of it, and Hauer rewrote Roy's "tears in rain" farewell himself and brought it to Scott on set the day it was shot. Seven versions exist. The 1992 Director's Cut removed the voice-over and the happy ending and put the unicorn dream back in; the 2007 Final Cut is the only version over which Scott had full artistic control, and it is the one to watch. It flopped and then became the film every dystopia since has been measured against - selected for the National Film Registry in 1993, named the second-most visually influential film of all time by the Visual Effects Society. IMDb 8.1.

suggestions.title: Inside Out
suggestions.description: Your animation shelf runs Spirited Away, My Neighbor Totoro, Grave of the Fireflies, Toy Story, WALL-E, The Lion King and Into the Spider-Verse - and this is the one that gets adults, which is the point. Pete Docter directed and co-wrote with Meg LeFauve and Josh Cooley, from a story he developed with co-director Ronnie del Carmen, for Pixar and Walt Disney Pictures. It began in October 2009 when Docter watched his own daughter, Elie, go quiet and withdrawn and wondered what was happening inside her; he and del Carmen then spent five and a half years building the answer, on roughly a $175 million budget, consulting the psychologist Paul Ekman (whose list of basic emotions supplied the cast) and Dacher Keltner of Berkeley, and half the story team were women at a time when the animation industry largely was not. It is set almost entirely inside the mind of an eleven-year-old girl, Riley (Kaitlyn Dias), whose family has moved from Minnesota to San Francisco, and the characters are her emotions: Amy Poehler as Joy, Phyllis Smith as Sadness - the two who get lost together - with Bill Hader as Fear, Mindy Kaling as Disgust, Lewis Black as Anger and Richard Kind as Bing Bong, the imaginary friend she is outgrowing, a character the studio deliberately kept out of the marketing so that he would land as a surprise. Michael Giacchino wrote the score. It premiered out of competition at Cannes on 18 May 2015 to an eight-minute standing ovation, opened in the US on 19 June to $90.4 million - the biggest opening weekend an original film had ever had - and finished on $859.1 million worldwide as the seventh-highest-grossing film of 2015 and the best-reviewed studio film of the year. It won Best Animated Feature at the 88th Academy Awards and was also nominated for Best Original Screenplay; the National Board of Review and the AFI both put it in their top ten of the year. It is 95 minutes and it ends on an image that is genuinely difficult, which is the reason it belongs on this list and not just the family one. IMDb 8.1.
